title: Writing chords on newspaper; Booga-Rooga and the name Boogie-Woogie
summary: He explains his chord system learned from Miss Pittman, and says the walking-bass movement was called Booga-Rooga by Blind Lemon before Pinetop Smith's 'Boogie-Woogie'.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: you know, you see these guitar parts and banjo parts where they have the names of the chords, you know? All right, I devised a way that I could take a piece of newspaper and write the chords on a piece of newspaper. And then I learned the structure of the... what the tonic note was, and the seventh...well, I'd learned all that from Miss Pitman, you know. And I learned how to...passing tones, and playing blues and Boogie-Woogie movement, but we didn't call it that, you see. Walking bass...

No. The first time I heard it called Boogie-Woogie was when Pinetop Smith recorded for Mayo {Williams, 1929}* out of Chicago. But before that, that movement, that bass movement, Blind Lemon Jefferson played on his guitar. And he called it Booga-Rooga. So now I don't know how...I guess that sometimes, you know what I mean, sometimes inexplicable, how you can explain terms, descriptions falling in a certain category and becoming a certain thing, as it final result. But it was Booga-Rooga for Blind Lemon Jefferson. He played those movements, those Boogie-Woogie movements and those eighth notes, you know.
